Connor,

Thanks again for the demo last week. We're preparing architecture guidance for our private deployment (VPC in us-west-2) and want a short, pragmatic comparison of the three main onramp patterns you mentioned: VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and site-to-site VPN to our on-prem DC.

Key constraints / asks from our side:
- Single-digit ms round-trip latency for inference calls from our regional services
- PCI-scope data path must not traverse public internet (even transiently)
- We want the simplest ops model for our small NetOps team (2 people) and clear failover behavior
- Budget is a factor: please give high-level cost drivers rather than hard quotes

Can you provide a short write-up highlighting latency tradeoffs, operational complexity, security boundaries, and a recommended approach for an initial pilot (we'll expand later)? If there are any things we should pre-provision on our side (CIDR ranges, route reflections, MTU), call those out.

Also looped Maya (NetOps) who will review network requirements. Looking to decide by end of month.

Subject: Re: Redwood Private — networking options (peering / privatelink / vpn)

Alex / Maya —

Thanks for the clear constraints. Below is a concise, pragmatic synthesis oriented toward a pilot. I've attached a one-pager that summarizes the recommendations. High-level guidance first, then short primers per option.

Recommendation (pilot):
- Start with AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints) for the pilot if: you need strict interface-level isolation, minimal route changes, and can accept slightly higher per-GB costs.
- If your primary driver is lowest possible latency and you can coordinate cross-account VPC peering and CIDR planning, use VPC Peering for the pilot.
- Reserve S2S VPN as a fallback / DR path or when on-prem-only workloads must access inference (or for short-term lift-and-shift).

Why PrivateLink for many pilots:
- Security: traffic never transits the public internet and the service is presented as an ENI in your VPC; better for PCI boundary audits.
- Ops: fewer global route table changes; consumer VPC keeps control over egress and NACLs.
- Simpler to add per-service IAM & endpoint policies to restrict which accounts can connect.

Why Peering when low latency trumps everything:
- Direct L3 connectivity; typically lower RTT than PrivateLink because you avoid the extra hop through an endpoint ENI and NLB in the provider account.
- No per-connection interface costs; cost profile is driven by data transfer (cross-AZ) and inter-region if applicable.

Why S2S VPN is useful but limited for steady-state inference:
- Quick to stand up and good for on-prem burst or air-gapped environments.
- Encryption over the public internet; for strict on-prem PCI requirements you'd want to pair VPN with dedicated transit (Direct Connect) or MPLS.
- Latency and jitter can be variable; not recommended as the primary low-latency path.

Operational notes / pre-provision checklist (pilot):
- CIDR: avoid overlapping CIDRs between your VPC and Redwood's peered VPCs; if using PrivateLink this is less constraining but still recommended.
- MTU: when routing via VPN, ensure MTU path-MTU >= 1400 to avoid fragmentation with TLS and gRPC payloads.
- DNS: for PrivateLink we recommend configuring private hosted zones or endpoint-specific DNS entries — our one-pager shows sample records.
- Route propagation: with peering you'll need to share and propagate routes; PrivateLink reduces the number of route updates required.
- Failover: plan a secondary path (S2S VPN) for regional failover if your latency SLOs allow it; our console can automatically route to a fallback model variant.

Cost drivers (very high level):
- PrivateLink: per-endpoint hourly + per-GB data processing charges; cost rises with number of endpoints and traffic volume.
- Peering: primarily data transfer costs between AZs/regions and cross-account transfer if applicable.
- VPN: hourly tunnel cost + data transfer out; consider Direct Connect if you need stable low-cost large-volume transfer.

Next steps:
1) If helpful, Ben can run a quick latency micro-benchmark (3-hour lab) from a representative Starlift service into our us-west-2 pilot to quantify delta between PrivateLink and Peering.
2) If you prefer Peering, we'll need a short CIDR/route coordination call with NetOps to reserve ranges.
3) I'll drop the one-pager and a checklist (attached).

Quick clarifying notes from our infra side — Alex, Maya, a couple points we usually call out when deciding pilot configuration:

1) Cross-account peering considerations: if you want sub-ms delta, peering within the same AZ (and keeping inference instances local) gives the best numbers. But it forces us to coordinate AZ placement for the dedicated pool and you to accept a new route to reach our subnet.

2) PrivateLink scale: if you have many microservices that will individually call the model, consider consolidating through a small lateral proxy in your VPC to reduce number of interface endpoints. That lowers per-endpoint costs and reduces connection churn.

3) Monitoring & observability: with Peering you get normal VPC flow logs and you can place VPC traffic mirroring for deeper network captures. With PrivateLink the endpoint is an ENI in your VPC; flow logs still work but need to target the endpoint's security group. We'll share our recommended CloudWatch/Datadog dashboards.

4) Session stickiness / NAT: note that if your service uses NAT gateways and ephemeral source ports at scale, you may want to configure connection pooling at the client to reduce NAT exhaustion when going through PrivateLink.

If you want I can sketch a 30-minute runbook for the pilot (peering + PrivateLink fallback) and list exact permissions we'd need to initiate the connection from our side. Connor / Kimberly — does that align with what you planned?

Ben Carter
Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Redwood Inference
